title: I'm a new doctor with no savings. Should I invest in property or REITs?
excerpt: A 26-year-old waiting for his housemanship asks how doctors can build a portfolio and whether REITs could replace property. Sean says REITs are closer to shares, and to rush the learning, not the buying.

question.asker: From A, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: A, 26, is waiting for his housemanship placement in a government hospital, where take-home pay starts at about RM4,000 to RM4,500. He has no savings yet, lives with his parents, works part-time and may be posted to any state. He wants to know how doctors can grow a portfolio given their long studies, whether to buy an investment unit he might live in later, and whether REITs are an alternative to property.
question.text: How should a young doctor start investing, and can REITs replace buying property?

answer.quote: It's not a real estate alternative, it's a stock alternative.
answer.summary: Don't rush to buy: property needs active income and credit, and his will grow. Use the next few years to save, avoid upgrading his lifestyle with each pay rise, learn by investing small sums, and buy investment property first once he earns about RM7,000 to RM8,000 a month. REITs are fine, but they behave like shares, not property.

reasons.title: Income and credit drive property investing
reasons.body: Investors with seven or eight properties usually earn RM15,000 to RM20,000 a month. For Sean, property is a way to diversify wealth as income rises, not a quick money maker, so starting at 36 or even 46 is fine.

reasons.title: Lifestyle creep is the real danger
reasons.body: As pay rises, people upgrade cars, homes and habits and save nothing more. Putting the extra into something that pays cash flow, starting with dividend shares or fixed deposits, builds the habit.

reasons.title: Investment and own-stay homes differ
reasons.body: High-yield units sit near jobs, transport and malls, while good family homes are quiet and low density, where tenants rarely rent. Buying one to rent now and live in later usually does neither well, and his postings could take him anywhere.

reasons.title: REITs lack property's leverage
reasons.body: Malaysian REITs yield about 4.8% to 5% and trade like shares. RM50,000 put into a RM400,000 subsale with a RM360,000 loan can bring about RM19,200 a year in rent that covers the instalment, while the asset itself can grow, though it takes far more work.

actions: Build your emergency fund first, and keep your insurance in place.
Learn to invest with small amounts, such as dividend-paying blue chips, fixed deposits or REITs, while your income grows.
Hold your lifestyle steady as your salary rises, and save the difference.
Rent while your postings move you around, and buy your first investment property when your income reaches about RM7,000 to RM8,000 a month.
Choose investment units by yield near jobs and transport, not as a future home.
caveat: Property suits people willing to deal with agents, managers, contractors and tenants; if that doesn't suit you, REITs and other assets are reasonable choices. The leverage example assumes the rent covers the instalment, which Sean says to check before buying.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #236. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as Sean stated them in January 2024. Sean mentions that he holds a master's degree in real estate with a research paper on REITs.
